message.content:
The history of cannibalism in the United States is largely defined by extreme survival situations, sensationalized media reports, and rare instances of criminal pathology. Unlike some cultures where ritual cannibalism was historically practiced, cannibalism in the U.S. has almost exclusively been viewed as a profound taboo, often associated with the breakdown of social order.

Here is a quick rundown of the most notable chapters:

### 1. The Donner Party (1846–1847)
The most famous instance of survival cannibalism in American history occurred when a group of pioneers traveling to California became trapped by heavy snow in the Sierra Nevada mountains. Of the 87 members of the party, 42 died. Faced with starvation, the survivors resorted to consuming the bodies of those who had already perished. The event became a permanent fixture in American folklore, symbolizing the horrors of the frontier.

### 2. The Alferd Packer Case (1874)
Alferd Packer, a prospector in the Colorado Territory, led a group of five men into the San Juan Mountains during a harsh winter. Months later, Packer emerged alone, appearing well-fed. He eventually confessed to killing his companions, claiming it was in self-defense
